chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Implied Volatility Actually Means

lessons.title: Why IV Is Not a Directional Forecast

children.text: Watch any trading desk chat on a day when India VIX jumps sharply and you will see some version of the same line: "IV is spiking, this thing is about to crash." It sounds like informed reasoning. It is actually a category error. Implied volatility answers the question how big a move is priced in. It has no opinion, mathematically, on the question which way. Those are two different questions, and only one of them is what IV was ever built to answer.
What IV Mathematically Encodes: Magnitude, Not Direction

Go back to the expected move formula from Lesson 1. It produces a single band around the current spot price, the same distance above as below. Nothing in the formula tilts that band upward or downward. It is a statement about dispersion, how wide the range of likely outcomes is, not about which half of that range is more probable.

body.latex: \text{Expected range} = \big[\, S - S \cdot IV \cdot \sqrt{T/365}, \;\; S + S \cdot IV \cdot \sqrt{T/365} \,\big]
body.caption: The same move size, S times IV times the square root of (T divided by 365), is added on the upside and subtracted on the downside. IV alone gives you the width of this band, not a lean toward either edge.

children.text: Plug in the Lesson 1 numbers: Nifty at 24,800, a normal week's IV giving an expected move of roughly ₹481. That produces a band of roughly 24,319 to 25,281. A trader reading that number as "the market expects a fall to 24,319" is inventing a lean that the arithmetic never put there. The honest reading is: the market is pricing roughly a two-in-three chance Nifty stays somewhere inside a ₹962-wide band by expiry, split evenly on both sides. Whether it lands nearer the top or bottom of that band is a completely separate question that plain ATM IV does not answer (Chapter 2, on skew, is where the market actually starts expressing a directional lean, through the relative pricing of different strikes, not through the ATM IV level itself).
Put-Call Parity: Why Calls and Puts Share the Same IV

There is a clean, no-arbitrage proof that IV cannot be a directional bet, and it comes from put-call parity. For European-style options on the same underlying, strike, and expiry, the call price and the put price are locked together by a fixed relationship. Nifty and Bank Nifty index options are European-style and cash-settled, which makes this relationship hold cleanly; individual stock options in India are American-style and physically settled, which adds minor complications this lesson sets aside.

body.caption: C is the call price, P is the put price, S is spot, K is strike, r is the risk-free rate, T is time to expiry in years. The right-hand side involves no volatility at all. It is fixed the instant S, K, r, and T are known.

children.text: Continue the Lesson 2 example: Nifty and strike both at 24,800, 7 days to expiry, r at 6.5%. The right-hand side works out to S minus K times e to the power of minus rT, which is 24,800 times (1 minus 0.9988), about ₹30.90. Lesson 2 solved a 10.85% IV from a ₹165 call price. Parity then pins the put price to 165 minus 30.90, about ₹134. If you solved for IV from that ₹134 put independently, you would get 10.85% again, the same number, because parity forces it to be. A call betting on "up" and a put betting on "down" are priced off one shared volatility number precisely because that number is not describing direction at all.

body.caption: Consistency check: same strike, same expiry, same IV (continuing the Lesson 2 example)

body.text: If calls and puts on the same strike ever implied meaningfully different volatilities with no dividend or borrowing-cost explanation, that gap itself would be a risk-free arbitrage: buy the cheap side, sell the expensive side, and lock in the mismatch. Parity holding in practice is the market's own proof that IV is a shared, direction-agnostic number, not a call-side or put-side opinion.

children.text: Then Why Does IV Spike When Markets Fall? The Leverage Effect

Here is the part that trips people up, and it is a fair confusion, because it is grounded in something real. India VIX genuinely does tend to rise more sharply during sharp Nifty selloffs than during equally sized rallies, and VIX has genuinely earned its "fear gauge" reputation. That is a real, well-documented pattern. It is just not evidence that IV encodes direction.

What is actually happening has a name: the leverage effect. As an index or stock falls, the same amount of debt in the underlying companies now sits against a smaller pool of equity value, which mechanically makes that equity riskier and pushes its volatility up. Layer on the behavioral side: sharp falls trigger urgent, price-insensitive demand for downside protection, margin calls, and forced deleveraging, all of which happen fast and push option premiums, and therefore the IV solved from them, up quickly. Rallies rarely trigger anything as urgent, so IV tends to drift down slowly on the way up and spike sharply on the way down. That asymmetry is a statistical regularity in how markets behave under stress. It is not a property built into the Black-Scholes formula, and it is not something IV is mathematically designed to signal.

body.title: Illustrative Pattern: Nifty Daily Return vs India VIX Daily Change

children.text: Notice the asymmetry in that illustrative pattern. Day 2's rally of similar size to Day 3's fall barely moved VIX, while Day 3's selloff spiked it sharply. That lopsidedness is real and worth internalizing. But it describes how large IV moves tend to be given a move's direction and speed, after the fact. It still does not mean a rising IV, by itself and in advance, is telling you which way Nifty is about to go.

body.text: Treating "VIX is up" as equivalent to "sell now, a crash is coming" confuses a historical tendency (falls tend to spike VIX harder than rallies) with a forward-looking signal. VIX rising tells you the market is currently pricing more uncertainty. It does not tell you which direction that uncertainty will resolve in.

body.title: Reading a VIX spike correctly
body.question: India VIX jumps from 13 to 22 over two sessions while Nifty is roughly flat. A trader concludes: "VIX only spikes when the market is about to crash, so I should sell my long positions." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: There is no flaw; a VIX spike always precedes a crash

VIX rising means options are pricing a bigger expected move in either direction, not specifically a fall; the tendency for VIX to spike harder in selloffs than rallies is a separate behavioral pattern (the leverage effect), not a built-in directional signal
VIX cannot rise unless Nifty has already fallen
VIX only reflects call option prices, so it cannot say anything about downside risk
body.explanation: IV, and VIX as its market-wide aggregate, is built from both calls and puts and is direction-agnostic by construction, as put-call parity shows. It rises because a bigger move is priced in, not necessarily a bigger fall. VIX's tendency to spike harder in selloffs than in equivalent rallies is a real, separate empirical pattern (the leverage effect and panic put-buying), layered on top of IV's core definition, not a mathematical property of IV itself.

body.title: Suvidha Labs and the USFDA verdict
body.scenario: Suvidha Labs, a hypothetical mid-cap pharma company, has a USFDA facility inspection outcome due in 3 trading days. The stock has traded in a tight ₹8 range around ₹640 for weeks, keeping realized volatility very low, but its at-the-money options are pricing an implied volatility of 68%, against a normal level of around 30% for this stock. A trader buys an ATM straddle (one call plus one put) ahead of the announcement, reasoning that such sharply elevated IV must mean the market expects the stock to fall on bad news.
body.prompt: Is the trader's reasoning correct? Explain what the elevated IV is actually signalling, and what determines whether the straddle makes money.
body.modelAnswer: The trader's reasoning is wrong. An IV of 68% against a normal 30% says the options market expects a much larger move than usual, in either direction; it says nothing about whether that move is more likely to be up, on a clean inspection, or down, on a warning letter. Because this is an ATM straddle, the call and put are priced off the same shared IV, so the position profits from the size of the move, not its direction, as long as the actual move exceeds the combined premium paid for both legs, a premium that is expensive precisely because IV is elevated. A sharp gap up on approval can pay off the straddle exactly as well as a sharp gap down on rejection. The real risk is IV crush after the announcement: even a fairly large move can still lose money if it turns out smaller than what the sharply elevated 68% IV had already priced in.

body.title: What Elevated IV Tells You vs What It Does Not

columns.label: What elevated IV tells you
points: The market expects a larger move than usual before expiry
Options (calls and puts alike) are more expensive to buy and more valuable to sell
A wider expected range around the current spot price
Possibly a known event, or genuine uncertainty, sitting ahead on the calendar

columns.label: What elevated IV does not tell you
points: Whether the move is more likely to be up or down
That a crash, specifically, is coming
Anything about the shape or skew of that expectation (that is Chapter 2)
The direction a rising VIX will resolve in, even though VIX often spikes harder in selloffs than rallies

body.text: Implied volatility prices the size of the storm, not which way it blows. Calls and puts share the same IV at a given strike because IV was never a bet on direction to begin with, and the well-earned reputation of VIX as a fear gauge comes from how sharply it tends to react to selloffs, not from anything in its definition that forecasts one.

points: IV measures the magnitude of an expected move (dispersion), not its direction; the expected move formula adds the same distance above and below spot.
Put-call parity (C − P = S − Ke^(−rT)) forces calls and puts at the same strike and expiry to imply the same volatility, since any persistent gap would be a risk-free arbitrage.

Nifty and Bank Nifty options are European-style and cash-settled, which lets parity hold cleanly; individual stock options in India are American-style and physically settled, adding minor complications.

The leverage effect explains why IV (and India VIX) tends to spike harder in selloffs than in equally sized rallies: this is a behavioral and mechanical market regularity, not a property built into IV's mathematics.
A rising VIX means the market is pricing more uncertainty right now. It is not, by itself, a forecast of which direction that uncertainty resolves in.
